1.explanation: To add a secondary style variant you must update the React <Tabs> component and the core Tab implementation. In Tabs.js the Tabs class’s propTypes and defaultProps need a new 'variant' or 'secondary' prop, and the render() function needs to inject a new CSS class (e.g. `${prefix}--tabs--secondary`) via classNames. In the vanilla-JS Tab class (tabs.js) the static options getter defines the CSS class names and selectors; it must be updated to include the new modifier class so that the secondary style is applied consistently at the core level.
1.bug_scenario: The screenshot shows two horizontally laid-out tabs: “Application Discovery” on the left (active) is rendered in the primary blue color with an underline, and “Enterprise Artifacts” on the right (inactive) is a light grey. The user wants a secondary style variant where the active tab uses a different (secondary) color or underline style, matching their custom-tabs.css, and have that built into the Tabs component.

2.explanation:
1. In the React wrapper (packages/react/src/components/Tabs/Tabs.js) the Tabs class and its render() method are responsible for building the outer <nav> and <ul> elements and applying the Carbon CSS classes via classNames. To support a secondary style, you will need to add a new prop (e.g. `kind="secondary"`), update propTypes/defaultProps, and modify render() so that it applies an alternate set of classNames (for example `${prefix}--tabs--secondary`) when that prop is present.

2. In the vanilla JS implementation (packages/components/src/components/tabs/tabs.js) the Tab class’s static options define all of the CSS selectors and class names used for rendering tabs and the dropdown trigger. To allow a secondary variant, you will need to extend these options (or introduce a new option) so that the markup it produces can switch to a secondary set of CSS classes (for example `${prefix}--tabs--secondary`, `${prefix}--tabs__nav--secondary`, etc.).

By updating both the React wrapper and the underlying vanilla implementation, the library can ship a built-in secondary styling option rather than relying solely on external overrides.
2.bug_scenario: The user wants to add a new “secondary” styling option to the Tabs component (as shown in the screenshot), so that tabs can render with a light‐grey background, subtle borders, and blue text/underline for the active tab. They currently have only the default Carbon primary styling available and are overriding via an external CSS file – but would like the library itself to support “secondary” style out of the box.
